sysd-msg-047.title: Waiting for a reply versus carrying on
sysd-msg-047.text: Ask a web server for a page and you wait until it answers. That is synchronous communication, the way HTTP works: the sender waits for a reply. In asynchronous communication the sender carries on without waiting. Waiting is not always the right choice. An application may only need to tell another that an event occurred, and a sender should not stall because a recipient has crashed. Most applications mix the two: an interactive one can answer part of a request at once and queue other parts, such as billing, to be done later. A subsystem that performs message queuing, or broadcast messaging, can improve the whole system's behavior in these situations, and {{ref:sysd-msg-046}} shows how. It can even be layered over a synchronous request-response protocol, as some queue services do over HTTP. The underlying protocol then limits what they can offer.

sysd-msg-056.title: Four kinds of queue, from plain to double-ended
sysd-msg-056.text: A queue takes new elements at one end and gives them back at the other. The simple kind is FIFO. A new element goes in at the tail and the oldest leaves from the head, so emails for payment responses go out in the same order. A circular queue, also called a ring buffer, links its last element to its first; LMAX's low-latency ring buffer runs in memory. In a priority queue, the element with the highest or lowest predefined priority is taken first. A deque, or double-ended queue, allows insertion and deletion at both ends, so it supports FIFO and LIFO.

sysd-msg-046.title: Message queues: leave it with the queue and move on
sysd-msg-046.text:
A message queue lets two programs talk without ever being busy at the same moment. The sender drops a message in and moves on, and the queue holds it until the receiver takes it. It is a software component, typically used for communication between processes or threads. It is the working form of the asynchronous idea in {{ref:sysd-msg-047}}, because neither party needs to touch the queue at the same time as the other. The paradigm is a sibling of the publisher/subscriber pattern and is typically one part of a larger system of messaging middleware, described in {{ref:sysd-msg-138}}.

In practice an administrator configures the queue-manager or broker software and defines a named queue. An application registers a routine that listens for messages, and other applications connect and put messages onto the queue. The queue manager stores the messages until a receiving application connects, then calls the registered routine, and the application processes the message. Queues have implicit or explicit limits on the size of a single message and on how many may remain outstanding. Queuing systems that connect different computer systems typically add resilience so that messages do not get lost when a system fails. The software can be proprietary, open source or a mix, and it runs on private servers or as an external cloud service.

sysd-msg-138.title: Middleware that carries messages between systems
sysd-msg-138.text: Call a procedure on another machine and you wait until it returns. Message-oriented middleware offers a looser deal. It is software or hardware infrastructure that supports sending and receiving messages between distributed systems. It insulates developers from the details of operating systems and network interfaces, so independently developed components on different platforms can interact. Middleware built on remote calls ties components tightly, because the caller waits; the message-oriented kind lets them stay loosely coupled. The sender hands a message to the provider and carries on, confident the provider keeps it until a receiver retrieves it. If the receiver fails, senders continue unaffected while messages accumulate until it restarts. The provider can also store, route or transform messages in transit. The cost is an extra component in the middle, the broker of {{ref:sysd-msg-051}}, which can reduce performance and reliability and make the system harder and costlier to maintain. A sender can also keep piling work on a recipient until it fails, so message flow must be monitored and adjusted.

sysd-msg-050.title: At most once, at least once, exactly once
sysd-msg-050.text: How many times should a message reach its consumer? Once sounds right, yet it is the hardest answer to build. Delivery semantics name three choices: at most once, at least once, or exactly once. At-most-once means a message is delivered not more than once, so messages may be lost but are never redelivered. That suits use cases such as metrics gathered to monitor a system, where a small amount of data loss is acceptable. At-least-once loses no message but may deliver the same one several times. That is usually good enough when duplication is not a big issue. It is also fine when the consumer can deduplicate, for example by rejecting a duplicate write on a message's unique key. Most brokers offer at-least-once delivery, so consumers will eventually see duplicates. Exactly-once is the most difficult semantic to implement. It is friendly to users but costs a lot in performance and complexity. It matters for financial use cases such as payment, trading and accounting, especially when duplication is unacceptable and the downstream service does not support {{ref:sysd-reliab-071}}.

sysd-msg-067.title: What a buffer between producers and consumers buys
sysd-msg-067.text: In a small system a write is predictably fast. In a large distributed one, the same write can take an almost non-deterministic amount of time. Queues are used to manage requests under that uncertainty, and putting a buffer between producers and consumers buys four things. The first is scalability: at peak load, multiple instances of an application can add requests to the queue without risk of collision, a theme from {{ref:sysd-scale-059}}. The second is decoupling, since queues remove dependencies between components and simplify decoupled applications. The third is performance: endpoints interact with the queue, not each other, so producers can add requests without waiting for them to be processed. The fourth is reliability, because queues make data persistent and reduce the errors that happen when parts of the system go offline.

sysd-msg-049.title: From closed vendor protocols to open standards
sysd-msg-049.text: Message queuing began on closed, proprietary protocols. Sun's JMS specification offered only a Java-only abstraction of a client API. Three open standards now serve open source queues. The first is AMQP, feature-rich and approved as ISO/IEC 19464 since April 2014; {{ref:sysd-msg-136}} goes deeper. The second is STOMP, a simple, text-oriented protocol. The third, {{ref:sysd-msg-137}}, is lightweight and aimed especially at embedded devices. AMQP and STOMP operate at the same level as HTTP, while the lightweight one operates at the level of TCP/IP. Some proprietary implementations, such as Amazon's SQS, use HTTP itself, but they stay constrained by that protocol.

sysd-msg-051.title: The broker that sits between sender and receiver
sysd-msg-051.text: A sender should not have to know where its receiver is, whether it is running, or how many receivers there are. A message broker takes on that knowledge. It is an intermediary program that translates messages between the messaging protocols of sender and receiver and validates, stores, routes and delivers them. Because it translates from the sender's formal protocol to the receiver's, services written in different languages or on different platforms can talk to each other. Because it stands in the middle, it decouples processes and services. A broker may manage a workload queue or message queue for several receivers, with reliable storage, guaranteed delivery and perhaps transaction management. It offers two basic distribution patterns: point-to-point messaging, as in queues, and publish-subscribe messaging, where producers publish to topics that consumers subscribe to. Brokers are generally built on one of two architectures: hub-and-spoke, where a central server provides integration services, or a message bus acting as a communication backbone.

sysd-msg-136.title: AMQP, the protocol that standardizes the bytes
sysd-msg-136.text: Most messaging standards describe an API. AMQP describes bytes. It is an open standard application layer protocol for message-oriented middleware. Because it is wire-level, any compliant tool can interoperate with any other regardless of language, unlike API-level standards such as JMS. It is a binary protocol that assumes a reliable transport such as TCP. It offers flow-controlled messaging with at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once guarantees, plus encryption and identity checks based on SASL and TLS. Messages travel one way over a link in transfer frames, and credit-based flow control keeps a receiver from being overwhelmed. Every transferred message must eventually be settled, so sender and receiver agree on its state; that settlement is how the guarantees are enforced. The bare message stays immutable in transit, so end-to-end signing, encryption and integrity checks stay valid. Version 1.0 focuses on the core features Internet-scale interoperability needs, with less explicit routing than earlier versions. Implementations include Apache Qpid, ActiveMQ, Solace and the 4.0 release of {{ref:sysd-msg-072}}.

sysd-msg-072.title: RabbitMQ: an Erlang broker that learned many protocols
sysd-msg-072.text: RabbitMQ began as an implementation of one protocol and now speaks several. It is an open-source message broker that originally implemented AMQP and has been extended through a plug-in architecture to support STOMP and other protocols. The server is written in Erlang and built on the Open Telecom Platform framework for clustering and failover. Client libraries exist for all major programming languages. Plug-ins add more: Shovel moves or copies messages from one broker to another, Federation shares messages between brokers, and Management monitors and controls brokers and clusters. RabbitMQ uses Raft to implement durable, replicated FIFO queues. System designs often place jobs on a queue such as Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ, for example for notifications, video processing and extracting transactions from accounts.

sysd-msg-139.title: ActiveMQ: a Java broker that speaks many protocols
sysd-msg-139.text: ActiveMQ is a Java broker that does not leave everyone else out. It is an open source message broker written in Java with a full Java Message Service client; Java applications use JMS 1.1 and other languages use cross-language clients. It supports several transport protocols, among them OpenWire, STOMP and AMQP. ActiveMQ Classic gets high availability from file-system or database row-level locking, a shared persistence store, or replication using ZooKeeper, and it scales horizontally with a Network of Brokers. Artemis, based on the HornetQ code base, is the next-generation broker under the ActiveMQ umbrella: multi-protocol, embeddable, clustered and asynchronous.

sysd-msg-048.title: Choosing a queue's semantics: durability, expiry, filtering
sysd-msg-048.text: A queue is a menu of choices, and several of them affect reliability and efficiency. Durability decides where messages live: in memory, on disk, or even in a database. Queues or messages may have a time to live (see {{ref:sysd-blocks-028}}), and some systems filter data so a subscriber sees only messages matching pre-specified criteria. Delivery policies decide whether a message must arrive at least once or no more than once, as {{ref:sysd-msg-050}} explains. Routing policies decide which servers receive a message when there are many queue servers. Batching policies and receipt notification for publishers also have substantial effects on transaction semantics, reliability and efficiency.

sysd-msg-058.title: Queues that live inside the operating system
sysd-msg-058.text: Not every queue crosses a network. Many implementations work only inside an operating system or an application, for that system's purposes alone. UNIX has two common ones: one in the SYS V API and a later, similar one in POSIX. In SYS V, a blocking receive puts the caller to sleep until a message of the requested type is posted. A non-blocking receive returns at once to report that it failed. Graphical user interfaces use the same idea. A message queue, also called an event queue, passes mouse, keyboard and timer events to the application, which removes them one at a time in an event loop.

sysd-msg-135.title: Amazon SQS: queuing over HTTP
sysd-msg-135.text: In Amazon's Simple Queue Service, neither the number of queues nor the message traffic has a limit, yet a single message body may not pass 256KB. SQS is a distributed queuing service, and messages can be of any type. It queues over HTTP: asynchronous behavior can always be layered over request-response semantics, but such a service is constrained by the underlying protocol. Its FIFO queues guarantee ordering within a message group, though not necessarily across retries or failures. A larger message can be split into segments, or stored in Amazon S3 or DynamoDB with only a pointer sent in the SQS message.

sysd-msg-134.title: Dead letter queues for messages that will not go through
sysd-msg-134.text: One message that can never be processed can clog a queue. A dead letter queue is where a messaging system stores messages it cannot or should not deliver. Depending on the implementation, a message lands there if its queue does not exist or its time to live expires. It also lands there if another exchange rejects it, or if it was read and rejected too many times. Setting them aside lets the main queue keep moving. They can be inspected later, without blocking processing or wasting CPU cycles on a message that may never succeed. Studying them reveals common fault patterns and software problems. A consumer that finds a message invalid can forward it to an Invalid Message Channel, separating application-level faults from delivery failures. Managing these queues means watching them, raising alerts, and adding handlers for automated or manual remediation. In an SQS FIFO queue, later messages in a group wait until the preceding one is processed or moved to the dead-letter queue. There it is no longer retried, leaving a gap while the others continue in order.

sysd-msg-069.title: Seven features most message queues offer
sysd-msg-069.text: Open the feature list of almost any queue and the same items turn up. Message queues commonly offer delayed delivery, delivery guarantees, dead-letter queues, ordering, poison pills, identity checks and task queues. Many queues let a message carry a specific delivery time, and a delay queue gives all messages a common delay. Queues may store multiple copies for redundancy and resend messages after failures to deliver at least once, while FIFO queues filter out duplicates automatically to deliver exactly once. A dead-letter queue receives messages other queues cannot process, as {{ref:sysd-msg-134}} describes. Most queues give best-effort ordering: messages are generally delivered in the order sent and at least once. In a FIFO queue the oldest entry, the head, is processed first. Poison pills are special messages that can be received but not processed. They signal a consumer to end its work, much like closing a socket in a client/server model. Queues check the identity of applications that try to access them, which allows messages to be encrypted over the network and in the queue itself. Task queues receive tasks and their data, run them and deliver the results, can support scheduling, and can run computationally intensive jobs in the background.

openers.msg: Ask a web server for a page and you wait for the reply. That is synchronous communication, as with an HTTP request; in asynchronous communication the sender carries on without waiting. This part begins with the second kind. A queue holds messages until the receiver takes them, and an intermediary program translates, stores, routes and delivers them between systems. With such a buffer between producers and consumers, a system can scale, decouple its components, respond faster and survive failures.
openers.message-queues-and-brokers: A queue is a widely used data structure: it takes new elements at one end and gives them back from the other. Turn it into a software component between programs and it becomes a place where messages wait until the receiver is ready. This chapter follows that idea from the common variants of the queue to the intermediary programs, open protocols and open-source software built around it. One question keeps returning along the way: how many times does a message reach its consumer, at most once, at least once, or exactly once?
